title: Suman Kalyanpur Spent Her Last Days Listening to Her Own Songs. Then Bollywood's Golden Voice Went Silent at 89.
excerpt: The Padma Bhushan singer recorded thousands of tracks in Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, and six other languages across six decades. She was laid to rest in Mumbai with state honours. The film industry largely did not show up.
body:
She spent her final days at home in Lokhandwala, Mumbai, listening to her own recordings. On the evening of May 31, around 8 pm, Padma Bhushan Suman Kalyanpur — the voice behind Aajkal Tere Mere Pyar Ke Charche, Na Na Karte Pyar Tumhin Se, and Tumne Pukara Aur Hum Chale Aaye — passed away peacefully from age-related causes. She was 89.

The next day, her mortal remains were wrapped in the Indian tricolour at the Santacruz Pawan Hans crematorium in Mumbai. Mumbai Police officers gave a ceremonial salute. Her daughter, Charu Agny, performed the last rites as a small gathering of loved ones sang Rahen Na Rahen Hum, Meheka Karenge from the 1966 film Mamta while the funeral pyre was lit.

The Bollywood industry largely stayed away.

The Voice That Was Always There

Suman Kalyanpur's career is one of those Indian music stories that is both celebrated and inadequately acknowledged. Born as Suman Hemmadi, she began recording in the early 1950s — first for All India Radio, then for Marathi cinema, and by 1954, for Hindi films. Over the next three decades, she lent her voice to an astonishing range of films and composers: Shankar Jaikishan, Madan Mohan, S.D. Burman, Naushad, Laxmikant-Pyarelal, and Kalyanji Anandji all sought her out.

Her voice occupied a specific frequency in Hindi cinema's golden age — clear, melodic, technically precise, and emotionally transparent. It was also, by her own admission, close enough to Lata Mangeshkar's that confusion was common. Radio Ceylon, which did not announce singer names during song relays, compounded the problem. "I was quite influenced by her," Kalyanpur told The Indian Express in a 2015 interview. "Meri aawaaz nazuk aur patli thi. Also, when Radio Ceylon relayed the songs, the names were never announced. Even the records sometimes gave the wrong name."

More Than Hindi

What set Kalyanpur apart was her multilingual range. She recorded in Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Kannada, Assamese, Gujarati, Odia, Bhojpuri, Rajasthani, and Punjabi. Her Marathi songs — Ketakichya Bani Tithe, Sang Kadhi Kalnar Tula, Nimbonyachya Jhadamaghe — are classics that remain on the lips of Maharashtrian audiences today. Union Minister Nitin Gadkari, in his tribute, specifically named these tracks before describing her passing as "a great loss to the Indian music world."

Beyond film music, her repertoire included devotional songs, ghazals, and thumris. She was not a performer who sought the spotlight or cultivated public controversy. She recorded, she sang, and the songs endured.

The Diaspora Connection

For the Indian diaspora, Suman Kalyanpur's songs belong to a particular kind of memory — the kind that lives in parents' and grandparents' playlists, in the background of family gatherings, in the music that played during long car rides in the 1990s and 2000s when first-generation immigrants kept Hindi film music alive in their new countries. Aajkal Tere Mere Pyar Ke Charche is not a song many young NRIs can name by title, but it is a melody most would recognise within three notes.

Her passing, coming at 89 after a career that spanned six decades, was not unexpected. But the absence of the film industry at her cremation — noted by multiple journalists covering the event — underscored an uncomfortable pattern in Bollywood: artists who define eras are mourned with social media posts and then, within a news cycle, forgotten.

Legacy

Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis described her death as "the loss of a divine voice." NCP chief Sharad Pawar said it "marked the end of a golden era." Deputy CM Eknath Shinde called her "an enduring symbol of Indian light classical and film music."

Suman Kalyanpur is survived by her daughter, Charu. Her songs are survived by everyone who has ever heard them.

Sources: Bollywood Hungama, Pinkvilla, Filmfare, LiveMint, The Hindu Business Line
author: Diaspora Desk
